name: Lena Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a fabric-dyeing line and check the first dried strip against the order. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the strongest workers at judging shade and temperature, though I still use a written run sheet. A wet blue roll can tell a false story until it dries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Iqbal tends school grounds, and our grown children live separately. We have a mortgage, five months of expenses saved, my typical operator pay and some similar dye houses nearby. I have never used AI; I ask for a person to show me required forms in paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the fabric-dyeing crew that small office shortcuts are all right if they do not skip the first colour check. A blue that looks right in a tank can dry grey on the cloth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the dyeing line and know how the cloth changes under heat, but I am paid the ordinary operator rate. My partner Iqbal tends school grounds, our grown children live on their own, and five months saved gives us some room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the dyeing shift, check a dried test strip against the order and record the temperature on paper. I would put a modest amount from each new full wage into savings after the mortgage and food were paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about a mostly unchanged job. The house bills are covered, and I can spend the evening tending our small garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dry a test strip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wet fabric can hide a shade error. I wait for the strip to dry before releasing the next roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. If a form changes, I need a person to show me during paid time without cutting normal weekly pay or hours.

I would ask for **paid personal instruction** if forms change.
think: Our **five-month reserve** covers a temporary setback.
Iqbal’s **groundskeeping wage** and my typical pay cover current mortgage bills.
do: Keep **fabric-dyeing shifts** and compare dried strips.
Record **vat temperatures** on the paper run sheet.
Save a **modest amount** from new full wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** with current work, wages and household costs.

fieldNote: Her **technical diploma** and exceptional dye skill support shift leadership at typical pay.
New **savings deposits** come from earned wages after bills; existing five months remain a separate cushion.

steps.text: Keep dye-line shifts and compare dried test strips
Save modest amount from new full wages after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can automate buying, but a robot lifting wet rolls needs a proper guarded test. We should be told what paid hours remain before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lifting robot could take a second operator from my shift and perhaps reduce my hours too. Five months saved helps, but some nearby dye houses may also change their crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management for a written rota and request an offered paid demonstration with the winch isolated and a qualified fitter beside us. I would watch if the place is real, then keep my paper shade checks; after an actual hours cut, I would apply for posted reachable dye-line jobs only where net pay after travel covers our mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing some wages, with time to compare options. A roll can be replaced; a hand caught in a winch cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run the new controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and watching a safe demonstration does not qualify me to operate a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any other dye house do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only one with an actual posting and weekly pay that works after travel. I would not exchange a known wage for a rumour.

feel: **Anxious** about plausible cuts to her own hours.

fieldNote: She asks for **safety and roster** terms without claiming robot operation.
The **observation** needs an offered paid place; job applications need cuts and adequate posted net pay.

steps.text: Request written dye-line paid rota from management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 reaches me at sixty, and capable cloth-handling robots around 2031 at sixty-three. The planning office changes before the wet rolls move themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to remove our late shift once robots can lift and inspect rolls. Iqbal’s school wage and five months saved would not cover the mortgage for a long search, and I wake at night thinking about the next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for dated staffing and severance terms and postpone the new greenhouse. If my shift ends, I would apply for posted reachable dye or finishing work at bill-covering net pay after travel and wait for a real offer and start date before leaving; if none appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about a large loss of wages. A perfect shade does not pay the house bill when the line is dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Iqbal’s confirmed wage covered the mortgage, food and health costs. We have not priced that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have homes and bills of their own. A lift to an interview might help, but I would not count their wages.

say: I would demand **dated staffing terms** before robot cuts.
I would ask for **written severance** if the late shift closes.
think: I expect **our late shift** to close around 2031.
The **mortgage and five-month reserve** make that a serious wage loss.
do: Request **dated dye-line staffing terms** and severance.
Postpone **new greenhouse** while wages are uncertain.
Apply after **shift closure** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Alarmed** and waking at night over expected major income loss.
S2.quote: A perfect shade does not pay the house bill when the line is dark.
fieldNote: Expected **late-shift closure** supports alarm despite a second wage and moderate savings.
Applications need **posted reachable work**, adequate net pay and a real offer before departure.

steps.text: Request dated dye-line staffing and severance terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three, and capable dye-line robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years might let the plant offer proper paid training in water testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and dye knowledge help, but testing treated water needs a recognised qualification and supervised sampling. Unpaid classes would strain the mortgage, and a certificate is not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid dye shift and ask for a funded paid-time water-testing course. If an actual place is offered with the treatment equipment isolated, a qualified tester supervising and a posted reachable testing role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about later work, yet able to check real course and wage terms. I would not sample a live chemical line to earn a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise the sampling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified tester would isolate the feed and show me safe collection on a training line. I would need the offered paid place first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted dye jobs if hours fell. I would not spend the five-month reserve on private fees.

I would require **posted local wages** before enrolment.
think: My **dye knowledge** helps but is not a water-testing qualification.
An **unpaid course** would strain our mortgage budget.

Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay testing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 reaches me at sixty-eight, and capable roll robots around 2039 at seventy-one. Ten years lets Iqbal and me price a last factory shift instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time work at sixty-seven, but five months saved is not retirement income. I do not know what any pension pays or whether Iqbal’s school hours will stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the dye shift and save a modest amount from new full wages after the mortgage and food. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots with today’s bills covered. I want to decide the last shift from a real household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the income falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted wages after travel if the shift shrank. A date cannot pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. I would share the decision with them, not budget their wages.

I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 roll robots.
think: Our **five-month reserve** cannot fund a long retirement with mortgage bills continuing.
A **sixty-seven exit** needs verified household income and remaining mortgage costs.
do: Keep **2026 dye shifts** and save from new full wages.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current bills are covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable roll robots around 2031 could close the late shift while the mortgage remains. Written staffing terms, offered funded paid safe water-testing training and posted reachable work with bill-covering pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask to see the first strip after it dries. A good dye run is measured on the cloth, not promised beside the vat.

headlineQuote: A good dye run is measured on the cloth, not promised beside the vat.
portrait: **Lena**, 58, leads fabric dyeing with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional shade judgment.
She has **typical pay**, school-grounds partner Iqbal, grown children, a mortgage, five months saved and some nearby dye houses.
She **never uses AI**, prefers paper checks and would retrain only through offered funded paid safe practical instruction.
Expected **2031 late-shift closure** alarms her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 roll robots may close the late shift while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
